articles.title: Boorman and the Devil review – enjoyable re-evaluation of the disaster that was Exorcist II: The Heretic
articles.summary: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned. David Kittredge gives us a thoroughly enjoyable, detailed account of the catastrophe that was John Boorman’s 1977 film Exorcist II: The Heretic, the…
body: According to an apocryphal tale gleefully repeated by William Friedkin, director of the first film, the sequel resulted in an enraged audience one night turning round and booing Warner Brothers executives in the back row of the cinema, and then chasing them out of the building and down the street. Boorman desperately recut the film with the sillier bits removed. But the damage was done.

Boorman is interviewed here and generously goes into great detail about his painful and mortifying experience with the film, how he had originally been offered the first Exorcist, disliked the story and turned it down, but was induced to take on the sequel. Perhaps Kittredge could have made it clearer how risky it was for Boorman to have taken on a project which he fundamentally didn’t believe in and was somehow creatively working against. He hired a kind of script-and-direction consultant, his friend Rospo Pallenberg, whose influence with Boorman annoyed the cast.
points: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned.

articles.title: ‘Today’ Snares Top Two Positions in Morning-News Battle for First Time in 14 Years
articles.summary: NBC’s “Today” is back on top in TV’s never-ending morning wars. The A.M. news franchise finished the 2025-26 broadcast season with the most viewers overall among morning programs and the most viewers between the ages of 25 and 54, the demographic most coveted by advertisers in TV-news content.
body: “Today” captured an average of 2.938 million viewers for the season, 4%, or 114,000 viewers higher, than audience levels at ABC’s “Good Morning America,” according to data from Nielsen, and 67%, or 1.174 million higher than viewership at “CBS Mornings.” Overall, the audience for “Today” rose by 7%, or 185,000 viewers, over the previous season.

“Today” won an average of 609,000 viewers between 25 and 54, 28%, or 134,000 more than “GMA” and 120%, or 332,000 more than “CBS Mornings.” It is the largest share of the demographic captured by the show in 15 years, according to data from Nielsen.

One ever-present dynamic of TV’s morning-news battle is that it never ends. “Today” will have to contend with not only its usual competition from “GMA,” but a new lineup at CBS, where Norah O’Donnell has rejoined the network’s A.M. team.
points: NBC’s “Today” is back on top in TV’s never-ending morning wars.

articles.title: Tom Cruise Is the Last Great Movie Star Still Chasing His Oscar. Can He Overcome ‘Digger’ Reviews to Get Him There?
articles.summary: Tom Cruise is going to divide us this year, and that might be the most interesting thing about his Oscar prospects for “Digger.” Depending on which screening you walked out of, it’s either the bravest swing of his late career or a miscalculation dressed up as one.
body: Before the festivals began, I posed a question: How divisive (or bad) would “Digger” need to be for Tom Cruise to lose this season? Venice, Telluride and Toronto have come and gone and now we approach the moment of truth. But there’s a more interesting question percolating — what will a Cruise Oscar campaign ask the Academy to recognize?

“Digger” stars Cruise as Digger Rockwell, a wealthy tycoon who must save the world when one of his oil rigs malfunctions and causes an environmental catastrophe across the planet. The film also includes Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons. The social embargo that lifted on Sept. 22 was mixed, with many praising Cruise’s performance but coming down hard on the film’s ultimate execution.
points: Tom Cruise is going to divide us this year, and that might be the most interesting thing about his Oscar prospects for “Digger.

articles.title: ‘Brace Your Heart’ Review: Tradition and Modernity Collide in an Impassioned Ode to Sámi Womanhood
articles.summary: For those of us who only ever think about reindeer when December draws in, and even then in a fairly abstract sense, “Brace Your Heart” arrives as a flinty reality check.
body: Amanda Kernell's third feature brings the identity politics of her debut, the historical drama 'Sámi Blood,' into the present day.

If Kernell’s screenplay can feel a bit schematic in its funneling of wider social issues into the small, hard story of one individual, “Brace Your Heart” is otherwise played with pleasing, powerful restraint — beginning with Valkeapää’s quietly expressive performance of a naturally taciturn character. Often shot in tight closeups that expose the harsh impact of the climate on her features, she’s frequently given the luxury of time to think on screen, particularly when weighing up crucial decisions on which the future and reputation of her entire family may depend.

articles.title: Disney+ and Hulu Raises Prices Again, the Fourth Hike in Four Years
articles.summary: The streamflation trend continues: Disney is once again asking Disney+ and Hulu subscribers to pay even more for the streaming service. Disney+ Premium and Hulu Premium, the plans without ads, are both increasing from $18.99 to $21.49/month.
body: The higher prices come as Pixar blockbuster “Toy Story 5” debuted on Disney+ on Wednesday. Variety has reached out to Disney for additional info.

Disney’s streaming price hikes have become an annual ritual. The latest increases mark the fourth time in four years the Mouse House is raising rates in the U.S., after price hikes for Disney+ and Hulu in October 2024 and in October 2023.
The ad-free Disney+ tier has now nearly doubled in price from the $10.99/month rate in 2023 prior to the fall increase that year.

articles.title: North Sea, Nature Untamed review – stunning footage finds the beauty and splendour under the water
articles.summary: Diver Peter van Rodijnen’s footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wilderness. The North Sea, with its cold grey waters, is the world’s drabbest.
body: First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea’s waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. He also brings us cute, coo-worthy stories from the depths; take the male shorthorn sculpin fish (no looker, it must be said) who spends the winter looking after his eggs, cleaning and blowing fresh water over them. Van Rodijnen’s camera is there for the baby fish hatching – pop, pop, pop out of their pearly plump pink eggs. There are some quirky stories, too, including a barnacle with a superlong penis.

body: After the trauma and burnout of tracking down Lecktor, Graham has been persuaded back on to the job by FBI chief Jack Crawford (Dennis Farina), desperate for his expert help; this has obvious implications for what no one in 1986 called Graham’s “mental health”. Graham is brilliant at the job because he can think his way into the serial killer’s twisted mind, and doing this all over again could send him over the edge. Right now, he has a very 80s-looking luxury sunkissed beachfront home in Florida in which to spend his retirement.

The Tooth Fairy himself is Francis Dollarhyde (Tom Noonan) who has a Frankenstein’s-monster type tendresse with a blind co-worker called Reba, played by Joan Allen. It is with her that the film has the strange and rather amazing, if preposterous, scene; somehow Dollarhyde has connections at the zoo which lets him get Reba in behind the scenes to stroke a sedated tiger in one of the most startling “first date” scenes in cinema.

articles.title: Angry Anderson, rock star who soundtracked Kylie's wedding in Neighbours, dies aged 79
articles.summary: He fronted the rock band Rose Tattoo, but became best known for his solo hit Suddenly.
body: Rock star Angry Anderson, whose music famously soundtracked the wedding of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan's characters in Australian TV soap Neighbours, has died at the age of 79.
The musician, whose real name was Gary Anderson, rose to fame as the frontman of Rose Tattoo, one of Australia's most revered rock bands, from 1976.

His solo song Suddenly became a global hit after it was played during the wedding of Minogue and Donovan's characters Scott and Charlene in Neighbours. The episode was watched by 20 million people in the UK in 1988.
Anderson said Minogue had been "adamant" that the track was used for the scene, and he later declared that Suddenly was the best song he had ever written.

articles.title: Remake review – Ross McElwee’s magnificent and moving tribute to a tragic loss and the art it inspired
articles.summary: Sherman’s March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art. This new film from revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee is an extraordinary work, arguably his most audacious use yet of autobiographical material while at the…
body: On that very simplest level, Remake starts out as a documentation of how Hollywood got in touch with McElwee and told him they wanted to make a fictionalised remake of his best-known film, Sherman’s March. Made in 1985 with a one-man crew (McElwee himself), Sherman’s March recorded the McElwee’s trip back to South Carolina where he grew up; there he films his family, old friends, and himself as he continually fails to establish romantic relationships with various women, all of it lavishly slathered with his own warm, softly southern-accented voiceover.

Remake slowly reveals what it was that led to Adrian’s death – not in order to create any kind of salacious mystery, but because it only makes sense, as much as something so senseless ever will, after we’ve got to know Adrian better: his aspirations and his troubles, a bipolar diagnosis, the deep wells of self-doubt that are not unlike his father’s. The end result is a profoundly moving work, one that will resonate with anyone who is a parent or close to a troubled kid, but one that has so much more about the making of art, its joys and its dishonesties. It lingers in the mind long after the tears have dried.
points: Sherman’s March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art.

articles.title: Jorja Smith 'very grateful' as she bags independent music prize
articles.summary: The singer reflected on her "crazy" journey as she collected the prize for best independent track.
body: Jorja Smith was among the artists recognised at this year's Independent Music Awards for her song The Way I Love You.
Accepting the award on Tuesday night at London's Roundhouse, Smith reflected on her "crazy" music journey and took a moment to mark the achievements of other artists.
"Everyone should be so proud," the Walsall singer said, especially those "doing everything independently".
Smith was visibly excited as she accepted her award on stage, while also encouraging the audience to applaud the other nominees and winners.

articles.title: Oasis add shows in Knebworth, Rome and Munich
articles.summary: The band says it is adding new dates after "phenomenal demand".
body: Oasis have announced more dates for the second leg of their reunion tour in 2027.
The band will now play six nights at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire, the 125,000-capacity venue where they staged two now legendary concerts in 1996.
They have also added shows in Munich and Rome, while their Paris dates have been rescheduled because of planned railway engineering works.
Tickets will not go on general sale. Instead, purchase links will be sent to fans who have already entered an online ballot.
